analysis.one_liner: Consolidates federal food safety into one independent agency with mandatory recall power.
analysis.headline: The Safe Food Act never received a hearing or a vote in either chamber; it died in committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, with three sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have pulled food safety duties scattered across at least 15 federal agencies — from USDA meat inspection to FDA food oversight — into a single independent Food Safety Administration. That agency would register and inspect food facilities on a risk-based schedule, set enforceable contaminant standards, order mandatory recalls, trace contaminated food back to its source, and police imported food through accredited foreign governments. It also added whistleblower protection and civil penalties of up to $250,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats: fewer foodborne illness outbreaks, faster and clearer recalls, better traceback when contamination happens, and tighter screening of imported food. The bill's own findings single out children, infants, older adults, and immune-compromised people as most at risk from lapses in the food supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially children and older adults

how_it_helps.text: Creates a single Food Safety Administration headed by a Senate-confirmed Administrator, consolidating food safety functions from USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service, FDA's food centers, and the seafood inspection program at Commerce — replacing a system the bill says involves at least 15 federal agencies.

Requires all food and feed facilities to register before operating or importing, and subjects them to risk-based inspection — continuous inspection of slaughter lines for the highest-risk category, down to annual inspection for storage facilities.

Gives the new agency mandatory recall authority with public notification, civil penalties up to $250,000 per violation (each day a separate offense), criminal penalties for knowing violations, and whistleblower protection for employees who report safety problems.
Establishes a national traceback system tracing food, animals, and ingredients from point of origin to retail sale, so outbreak investigations can find the source instead of guessing.

Tightens imported food oversight: foreign governments must be accredited to certify food for the U.S. market, importers must verify their foreign suppliers, and imported food is routinely inspected at the border.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry slaughterhouses and processors facing continuous or daily inspection, preventive process controls, and per-violation penalties; food importers and foreign suppliers facing verification and accreditation requirements; and warehouse and logistics firms that can be named in recall orders. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers in food prices.

drawbacks.text: Consolidating food safety functions from USDA, FDA, Commerce, and other agencies into one new agency is a large reorganization with real transition risk: the bill allows a 12-month transition period and requires a presidential reorganization plan, and mismanaged transfers have historically disrupted inspection staffing.

The enforcement regime is stiff — continuous inspection of every slaughter line during all operating hours, mandatory process controls, and civil penalties of $250,000 per violation with each day counted separately — costs that would fall hardest on smaller processors and could show up in grocery prices.

The bill concentrates significant discretion in a single presidentially appointed Administrator, including sole authority over recalls (which cannot be delegated) and the power to set alternative inspection frequencies for individual facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core case is strong: foodborne illness sicken tens of millions of Americans a year under a fragmented system the bill's own findings describe as outdated, and unifying it was a National Academy of Sciences recommendation. The consolidation and compliance costs are real but the kind an honest supporter would accept as the price of a safer supply chain; the main open question is whether one agency could absorb the transfer without disruption.

outcome.mechanism: DeLauro introduced it in October 2019; the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Agriculture Committees, a health subcommittee took it under review, and it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Safe Food Act of 2019 on October 18, 2019, joined by Rep. Grace Meng as the bill's other sponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Agriculture.
Three days later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
Only two House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and neither chamber's version ever reached the floor; the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors, food importers, and warehouse operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided new registration, inspection, recall, and traceback obligations. Consumers remain under the fragmented, multi-agency system the bill was written to replace.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll call exists; the bill's only support came from three House Democrats, and the Democratic chairs of both committees that held it took no action.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry processors and slaughterhouses
industries.note: The bill's highest-risk category covers slaughter, requiring continuous inspection of every slaughter line during all operating hours plus daily inspection, along with preventive process controls and per-violation civil penalties. The industry's interest in the bill's defeat ran against the public's interest in inspection and recall enforcement.

industries.industry: Food importers and foreign food exporters
industries.note: Importers would have had to verify foreign suppliers, foreign governments would need U.S. accreditation to certify food, and imports would face routine physical inspection — with detention, seizure, or denial of entry for noncompliant food. Cheaper, less-scrutinized imports are the cost the public pays today.

The bill explicitly did not exempt third-party warehouse and logistics providers from mandatory recall orders and required extensive records on food movement. Their exposure to recalls serves the public's ability to trace and remove contaminated food.

industries.industry: Food safety testing and technology providers
industries.note: The bill created a Food Safety Technology Program and required statistically valid sampling and testing, which would expand demand for detection methods and safety innovations. This interest runs alongside the public's interest in catching contamination earlier.
